newsitem.title: USA: Clinton takes offensive on campaign finance reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton takes offensive on campaign finance reform.

text.p: Working to stem criticism of Democratic fundraising tactics, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday challenged Republicans to agree to a bipartisan ban on large political contributions and accused them of accepting questionable donations as well.

At the same time, the White House said its legal counsel was completing new restrictions on who can gain access to the president to prevent a repeat of the situation last year when a Chinese arms dealer was among a group who attended a social gathering with Clinton.

Clinton came under heavy fire in the last months of the 1996 presidential campaign after revelations the Democratic Party had accepted large contributions from questionable sources, such as foreigners.

Democrats had to return more than $1.5 million, much of it raised by fundraiser John Huang, who tapped his contacts with Asian corporations to raise the funds. Asian-American businessman and Clinton supporter Charles Yah Lin Trie caused Clinton embarrassment when it was revealed he had brought Wang Jun, who heads a weapons trading firm owned by the Chinese government, to a White House social event last February.
A day after taking the oath of office for his second four-year term, Clinton attempted to satisfy critics that he would work toward campaign finance reform.
At the same time he invited scrutiny of Republican fundraising tactics, saying the opposition party had similar troubles but it was not getting the same attention from the news media.

"On the other side, our friends may not have any interest in campaign finance reform. Why should they? They raise more money. They raise more foreign money, they raise more money in big contributions, and we take all the heat. It's a free ride," Clinton said in a speech to the Democratic National Committee.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Republicans "should certainly acknowledge their errors as well." He said Republicans outspent Democrats by more than $200 million in last year's election campaigns.
Clinton said his party would stop accepting so-called "soft money" donations if the Republican Party would do the same.
These contributions are unlimited in size and are directed toward "party-building" rather than specific candidates, but critics say they give large donors undue influence on the political process.
Challenging Republicans to ban soft money, Clinton said: "If you will do it, we will do it. We have offered our hand again and again. Why not just say yes?"

Clinton also endorsed the reintroduction into Congress of a bipartisan bill to tighten rules for raising political funds sponsored by Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain and Wisconsin Democratic Sen. Russell Feingold.
"It is tough, it is balanced, it is credible. It should become the law of the land," Clinton said.

The bill does not ban soft-money contributions but imposes limits on them. McCain said in response to Clinton's appeal that he personally would be willing to accept limitations on soft money only if Democrats agreed to curb the contributions they receive from their labour union allies.

He also criticised Clinton for letting large donors stay overnight in the White House Lincoln Bedroom, a practice McCurry said Clinton would "absolutely not" change because Clinton is a "human being and is allowed to have guests in his residence."

McCain told CNN's Inside Edition: "I think that was an unfortunate speech by the president ... We never put out a 'For Rent' sign outside the Lincoln Bedroom. It was never Motel 1600 when President Bush and President Reagan were there."
